qs.q: What is a key movement impaired by injury to the median nerve at the wrist?
qs.e: Thumb opposition and abduction are impaired due to thenar muscle weakness following median nerve injury at the wrist. Ulnar nerve injury affects small hand muscles like interossei.
qs.s: Limb Anatomy Revision — Lower & Upper Limb: MCQs

qs.q: A patient experiences numbness in the lateral three and a half digits and weakness of the thenar muscles. Compression of the median nerve at the wrist typically occurs at which specific anatomical location?
qs.e: Median nerve entrapment at the wrist occurs within the carpal tunnel, deep to the flexor retinaculum, causing carpal tunnel syndrome. Guyon's canal is the site of ulnar nerve compression at the wrist.
qs.s: SDL Revision Mock Marathon — Upper Limb, Histology & Embryology —: MCQs

qs.q: In the upper limb, the median nerve gives off a specific branch in the forearm after passing between the two heads of pronator teres. What is this branch?
o: The lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm
qs.e: The median nerve enters the forearm between the two heads of pronator teres and gives off the anterior interosseous nerve. The posterior interosseous nerve is a branch of the radial nerve.
qs.s: SDL Revision Mock Marathon — Upper Limb, Histology & Embryology —: MCQs

qs.q: A patient presents with an inability to oppose the thumb and sensory loss over the lateral palm and first three digits. Which of the following intrinsic hand muscles is NOT supplied by the median nerve or its branches?
qs.e: The adductor pollicis is supplied by the ulnar nerve, whereas the other listed muscles are innervated by the median nerve. Opponens pollicis and the lateral lumbricals receive median nerve innervation.

qs.q: An orthopedic surgeon is reviewing potential sites of nerve entrapment in the upper limb. Which of the following is a recognized site of median nerve entrapment?
qs.e: The Ligament of Struthers is a known site of median nerve entrapment in the arm. The arcade of Frohse is associated with the radial nerve, while the arcade of Struthers relates to the ulnar nerve.

ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The median nerve runs from the brachial plexus through the forearm, innervating most hand flexors and the thenar muscles, and provides sensation to the lateral hand. It is clinically important for carpal tunnel syndrome and wrist injuries.

sections.p: The median nerve originates from the lateral and medial cords of the brachial plexus (C6‑T1). It travels down the arm, crosses the elbow, and enters the forearm between the pronator teres and flexor digitorum superficialis.
b: Carries motor and sensory fibers; supplies most flexors and the lateral hand.

sections.p: In the forearm, it lies anterior to the flexor digitorum superficialis and runs with the radial artery. At the wrist, it passes through the carpal tunnel.
b: Crosses the cubital fossa; enters the hand via Guyon’s canal.

sections.p: Medial to the brachial artery in the arm; lateral to the ulnar nerve in the forearm. At the wrist, it is adjacent to the flexor retinaculum.
b: Shares the carpal tunnel with the ulnar nerve and radial artery.

sections.p: The median nerve receives arterial input from the recurrent radial artery and the ulnar artery via the palmar arches.
b: Adequate perfusion is essential for nerve health; ischemia can cause neuropathy.

sections.p: Motor fibers innervate flexor carpi radialis, palmaris longus, flexor digitorum superficialis, flexor digitorum profundus (digits 2‑4), and most thenar muscles.
b: Sensory fibers supply the lateral palm and thumb.

sections.p: Controls wrist and finger flexion, thumb opposition, and provides sensation to the lateral hand.
b: Critical for grasp, fine motor tasks, and hand sensation.

sections.p: Common injuries include compression at the wrist (carpal tunnel syndrome), traumatic lacerations, and nerve stretch injuries.
b: Symptoms: numbness, tingling, weakness of thumb and index finger.

sections.p: On examination, a positive Tinel sign at the wrist and a weak thumb opposition suggest median nerve involvement.
b: Ask patients to oppose thumb and index finger; test sensation over the lateral palm.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe wrist pain with swelling, sudden loss of thumb function, or progressive weakness requiring urgent referral.
